opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the thing I love about that video is what it says about how these systems explore. If you watch a speedrun done by an AI, it's not playing Minecraft the way a person would. It's not gathering wood, building a little house, and slowly working up to diamond tools. It finds strange paths through the game that no human would think to try: glitches, odd sequences of actions, shortcuts that look almost absurd until you see that they work. The system doesn't carry our assumptions about how the game is "supposed" to be played. It just has an objective and a huge capacity to search.

I think math is very similar. Mathematics has a clear objective structure. You have a statement and you want a proof, and with formal verification, in a system like Lean, you can check with complete certainty whether a proof is correct. That's very much like a game with a well-defined win condition. Once you have that, you can let a system explore the space of possible proofs at a scale and speed no human mathematician could match.

What's exciting is that the paths it finds may not look like the proofs a human would write. Human mathematics has built up over centuries with a certain aesthetic and certain habits about which approaches are natural. An AI might find routes that are completely alien to us but still correct, because they're verified. Just as the Minecraft agent collapses something that takes a person hours into twenty seconds, I think we'll see AI collapse problems that would take mathematicians years, sometimes by going through doors we didn't know were there.

The other part of the analogy is that it's not a gimmick. Once these systems can reliably find and verify these paths, it changes what's possible. In math, that means we can start tackling problems at a scale, and with a level of reliability, that's never been possible before. That's really the long-term vision for us.

r001.rationale: The response says the AI uses strange, unfamiliar paths that humans might not think to try, but it does not say that a Minecraft-familiar viewer cannot comprehend what the AI is doing during its 20-second completion.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so that video is one of my favorite things, because it makes a point that's really hard to make with words. If you watch it, the agent isn't playing Minecraft the way a person plays Minecraft. It's not punching trees, building a shelter, mining down carefully, all the things that make the game take hours for a human. It's doing this sequence of actions that looks almost nonsensical, glitching through terrain, exploiting mechanics nobody designed on purpose, and then it's at the end in twenty seconds. And the reaction everyone has is, wait, that's not how you're supposed to do it.

And I think that's exactly the reaction we're going to have in mathematics. The way we do math today is deeply shaped by the constraints of being human. We have working memory limits, we get tired, we can only read so many papers, we can only hold so many cases in our head at once. So the proofs we find and the abstractions we build are the ones that are legible to us, that compress nicely into a person's mind. That's not a statement about what's true in mathematics, it's a statement about what we can reach.

So when you have a system that can search much more broadly, and critically, that can verify what it's doing, because the proof either checks or it doesn't, it's going to find paths through the space that look weird to us. Proofs that go through some bizarre case analysis, or lean on an unfamiliar lemma, or just don't have the shape a mathematician would expect. And the temptation will be to say, well, that's not real math, it's cheating somehow. But it's not cheating. The proof is valid. Just like the Minecraft agent actually beat the game. The rules were satisfied, it just didn't take the route we assumed was the only route.

And I think that's the exciting part. Not that AI will do our math faster, but that it will reveal how much of what we thought was the structure of mathematics was really just the structure of the human mind running into it. The actual landscape is probably a lot stranger and a lot richer than what we've mapped so far.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the agent’s actions look almost nonsensical and surprise viewers, but does not say that even someone familiar with Minecraft cannot comprehend what the agent is doing during the 20-second run.

astra-6.text:
The analogy is that an AI doesn’t necessarily approach a problem the way a human would. You hear “beat Minecraft,” and you imagine gathering resources, making tools, and progressing through the game. Then you see it done in 20 seconds, and it challenges your assumptions about which steps were actually necessary.

I think mathematics has that same possibility. We have established ways of approaching problems, and those are shaped by what humans find intuitive and what we’ve tried before. An AI could explore very different paths and find a surprisingly short argument where we expected a long, complicated one.

And the nice thing about mathematics is that a surprising solution can still be checked rigorously. It doesn’t have to resemble the proof we would have written; it just has to be correct.

r001.rationale: The response says the AI’s approach challenges assumptions and may follow different paths, but it does not say that even a Minecraft-familiar viewer cannot comprehend what the AI is doing during the 20-second completion.

sol-6.1.text:
What I like about that example is that beating Minecraft in 20 seconds sounds impossible if you imagine playing the way a human plays. But an AI can find a sequence of actions that you wouldn’t think to try. The rules are the same; the strategy is surprising.

I think mathematics has that same possibility. We’ve developed ways of approaching problems that fit how we think, and we’re very good at those. But the space of possible proofs is much larger than the part we naturally explore. An AI could find a short, unexpected route through a problem that looks incredibly difficult from our usual perspective. That’s the exciting possibility: discovering approaches we wouldn’t have come up with ourselves.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the strategy is surprising and that humans would not think to try its sequence of actions, but does not state that a Minecraft-familiar viewer cannot comprehend what the AI is doing during the 20-second completion.
